results.result: The manuscript establishes the context that stress-related disorders are a major global health burden, contemplative mental training can reduce stress and induce brain plasticity, but the specific types of mental practices most efficient for stress reduction and brain plasticity remain unclear.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C5 establish well-supported background context through appropriate citations to epidemiological data (C1-C2), meta-analyses and reviews (C3-C4), and identify a clear knowledge gap (C5) that motivates the current study. These are standard literature review claims appropriately supported by prior work.

results.result: The manuscript establishes that diurnal cortisol is an understudied marker in mental training research, and that cortisol is a key stress hormone and mediator of stress-disease relationships, with inconclusive evidence linking it to hippocampal structure.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C10 provide well-cited background on cortisol biology and its relationship to stress and hippocampal structure. The acknowledgment that findings are inconclusive (C10) appropriately frames the research gap. All claims are supported by appropriate citations to established literature.

results.result: The manuscript establishes that the hippocampus has high glucocorticoid receptor density, consists of functionally distinct subfields with unique microstructure and connectivity patterns, and plays a central role in HPA axis regulation, emotional reactivity, stress sensitivity, and stress-related disorders.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C23 provide comprehensive, well-cited background on hippocampal anatomy, function, and role in stress regulation. Each claim is supported by multiple appropriate citations to established neuroscience literature. This represents standard background knowledge appropriately documented.

results.result: The manuscript reviews prior evidence linking cortisol measures to hippocampal volume, noting both reduced CAR associated with smaller hippocampal volume and contrary findings of elevated cortisol associated with hippocampal atrophy, as well as associations between hippocampal functional connectivity and cortisol.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C29 appropriately review the mixed literature on cortisol-hippocampus relationships, citing both consistent findings (C24-C27) and contradictory evidence (C28-C29). The presentation of conflicting results is appropriate and well-documented, establishing the complexity of the relationship under investigation.

results.result: The manuscript establishes that mindfulness-based interventions like MBSR have gained popularity for mental health, can reduce stress and various cortisol measures, with prior work in the current sample showing reductions in hair cortisol through mental practice.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C37 provide well-cited background on mental training interventions and their effects on stress and cortisol. The inclusion of prior findings from the same sample (C36) is appropriately cited. All claims are supported by relevant literature including meta-analyses and empirical studies.

results.result: The ReSource Project investigated differential effects of three distinct 3-month mental training modules: Presence (attention/interoceptive awareness), Affect (socio-emotional skills including compassion), and Perspective (socio-cognitive skills including perspective-taking) on hippocampal subfields and cortisol.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C45 clearly describe the study design and training modules. The descriptions are consistent with the cited study protocol (Singer et al., 2016) and are well-documented in the methods section. The differentiation between training types is clearly articulated and forms the basis for the experimental design.

results.result: Prior work in the same sample found that socio-affective training specifically reduced CAR, socio-affective or socio-cognitive training reduced acute stress reactivity, all training types equally reduced hair cortisol, and the three modules induced differentiable changes in cortical structure and function.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C50 appropriately cite prior published work from the same research group and sample. These findings establish the context for the current investigation and are properly attributed to specific publications. The inference about training specificity (C49) follows logically from the cited evidence.

results.result: The study recruited 332 healthy adults randomly assigned to training cohorts (TC1, TC2) undergoing 9 months of sequential training modules in different orders, an active control cohort (TC3) receiving only Affect training, and a retest control cohort (RCC) with no training, with assessments at baseline and after each 3-month module.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C57 describe the study design with appropriate detail. The randomization, sample sizes, cohort assignments, and assessment schedule are clearly documented. This represents a well-designed longitudinal intervention study with appropriate control groups and counterbalancing of module order.

results.result: Affect training (vs. Perspective) led to relative increases in bilateral CA1-3 volume, with subtle increases following Affect and decreases following Perspective, no differences between Presence and active control, no overall 9-month change, and results robust to controlling for intracranial volume.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C63 report the primary structural findings with appropriate statistical details (t-values, p-values, effect sizes, confidence intervals). The right CA1-3 finding survives FDR correction (q=0.022), while bilateral findings are at p<0.05 uncorrected. The modest effect sizes (Cohen's D ~0.28-0.35) and lack of FDR correction for some comparisons warrant cautious interpretation, but the pattern is consistent and includes appropriate control analyses.

results.result: CA1-3 showed functional connectivity to default mode network regions at baseline. Right CA1-3 functional connectivity showed differential changes between Affect and Perspective training, with decreases following Perspective. Regional analyses revealed decreased left CA1-3 to posterior insula connectivity and increased right CA1-3 to mPFC connectivity when comparing Affect to Perspective.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C68 report functional connectivity findings with appropriate statistics. The baseline connectivity pattern (C64) is consistent with prior literature. The differential change in right CA1-3 network (C65) survives FDR correction (q=0.032). Regional findings (C67-C68) also survive FDR correction (q<0.05). However, the functional findings are less consistent than structural findings, with some effects driven by Perspective decreases rather than Affect increases.

results.result: Increases in bilateral CA1-3 volume following Affect training negatively correlated with reductions in total diurnal cortisol output (AUCg). Left CA1-3 functional connectivity changes positively correlated with diurnal slope and AUCg changes, with AUCg modulating connectivity between left CA1-3 and parietal-occipital cortex.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C73 report brain-behavior correlations with appropriate statistics. The CA1-3 volume-AUCg correlations (C69) approach but don't clearly survive FDR correction (q=0.05-0.056). The functional connectivity correlations (C71-C72) show one significant after FDR correction (slope: q=0.02) and one marginal (AUCg: q=0.052). The regional finding (C73) survives FDR correction. These correlational findings support the link between CA1-3 plasticity and stress reduction, though effect sizes are modest.

results.result: Increases in left CA1-3 volume and intrinsic function were consistently associated with decreases in hair cortisol, a marker of long-term stress exposure.
results.evaluation: Claim C74 reports associations between CA1-3 changes and hair cortisol with appropriate statistics that survive FDR correction (q=0.016-0.022). However, this analysis is based on a smaller subsample (N=44) and combines data across all training modules, limiting interpretation of training-specific effects. The finding is consistent with the diurnal cortisol results but should be interpreted cautiously given the reduced sample size.

results.result: Multivariate partial least squares analysis identified significant associations between cortisol stress markers and hippocampal plasticity, with Affect showing strongest associations with CA1-3 latent markers, and both slope and AUC changes showing strongest associations with the latent factor.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C76 report multivariate findings that survive FDR correction and show consistent patterns with univariate analyses. The PLS approach appropriately addresses the multivariate nature of the data and accounts for stability through permutation testing (1000 iterations) and bootstrapping (100 iterations). However, the manuscript could provide more detail on the specific contributions of individual variables to the latent factors.

results.result: The study demonstrates that compassion-based mental training alters CA1-3 structure, with training-based volume increases relating to decreases in total diurnal cortisol release, and CA1-3 functional changes associating with changes in diurnal cortisol slope, release, and long-term cortisol exposure.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C79 provide appropriate summary statements of the main findings. These are supported by the detailed statistical analyses reported in C58-C76. The conclusions appropriately acknowledge that causality cannot be definitively established despite the longitudinal design, and the authors appropriately discuss multiple potential mechanisms.

results.result: The hippocampus plays an inhibitory role in HPA axis regulation through abundant glucocorticoid receptors, making it susceptible to glucocorticoid neurotoxicity, with CA1 particularly susceptible due to NMDAR-associated synaptogenesis and CA3 vulnerable to glucocorticoid-induced damage.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C84 provide well-cited mechanistic background for interpreting the findings. All claims are supported by appropriate citations to established neuroscience literature. However, C84 cites animal studies (rodents, tree shrews), and the authors appropriately acknowledge uncertainty about translating these mechanisms to humans.

results.result: The mPFC plays a key role in HPA-axis regulation, with glucose metabolism negatively associated with stress-induced cortisol increases, and prior work showing structural changes in insular, opercular and orbitofrontal regions following Affect training in the same sample.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C87 provide relevant context for interpreting the functional connectivity findings, particularly the increased CA1-3 to mPFC connectivity. All claims are appropriately cited, with C87 referencing prior work from the same research group and sample, providing important context for the current hippocampal findings.

results.result: Prior work in the same sample showed that both Affect and Perspective training reduced acute cortisol reactivity, only Affect reduced CAR, and all training modules equally reduced hair cortisol over 3-9 months.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C90 appropriately cite prior published work from the same sample to contextualize the current findings. These citations are relevant for interpreting the specificity of training effects on different cortisol measures and help explain why some associations are found across training types while others are specific to Affect.

results.result: The study acknowledges that non-adherence to saliva sampling can significantly impact cortisol data, did not employ objective verification of sampling times, but addressed this through mobile phone-based experience sampling reminders.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C93 appropriately acknowledge a significant methodological limitation. The authors correctly cite evidence that non-adherence affects cortisol data and honestly report not using objective verification methods (e.g., electronic monitoring). The mobile phone reminder system partially addresses this concern but doesn't eliminate it. This transparent reporting of limitations is appropriate.

results.result: The study concludes that only the Affect training module (cultivating compassion and care) related to increases in CA1-3 volume with corresponding functional connectivity alterations and reduced diurnal cortisol output, with consistent alterations between cortisol change and CA1-3 volume/function across analyses, and multivariate analyses pointing to circuit-level understanding.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C98 provide appropriate summary conclusions supported by the detailed findings. The specificity to Affect training is supported by the comparative analyses (C58-C68), the brain-behavior correlations are documented (C69-C74), and the multivariate findings support circuit-level interpretation (C75-C76). However, the authors appropriately acknowledge in the discussion that some associations are present across training types, tempering claims of complete specificity.

results.result: MRI data were acquired on a 3T Siemens scanner, hippocampal subfields were segmented using a validated patch-based algorithm that has shown high accuracy in healthy populations and detecting pathology.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C101 describe the MRI acquisition and analysis methods with appropriate technical detail and citations. The segmentation algorithm is properly validated (Caldairou et al., 2016; Bernhardt et al., 2016). However, the authors appropriately acknowledge in the discussion that this approach has limitations, including potential over/underestimation of volumes and unclear subfield boundaries.

results.result: Cortisol was assessed from 14 saliva samples (7 per day) over two consecutive weekdays, taken at awakening and at 30, 60, 240, 360, 480, and 600 minutes post-awakening, and analyzed using time-resolved fluorescence immunoassay with 10/12% intra/inter-assay variability.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C104 provide detailed description of cortisol sampling and assay methods. The sampling schedule is appropriate for capturing diurnal cortisol patterns including CAR, slope, and total output. The assay method is properly cited and variability is reported. However, as noted in C91-C93, the lack of objective verification of sampling times is a limitation.

results.result: Hair samples were collected at each timepoint, with the proximal 3 cm segment analyzed to assess cortisol/cortisone accumulation over each 3-month period (assuming 1 cm/month growth), using liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C107 describe hair cortisol methods with appropriate detail and citations. The 3 cm segment for 3-month accumulation is based on standard assumptions about hair growth (Wennig, 2000). The LC-MS/MS method is appropriately cited as the criterion standard (Gao et al., 2016). The approach of analyzing samples from the same participant with the same reagent batch is good practice.

results.result: The study received ethical approval from University of Leipzig and Humboldt University Berlin, all participants provided written informed consent, and the study was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT01833104).
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C110 document appropriate ethical approvals, informed consent, and trial registration. The pre-registration at ClinicalTrials.gov is particularly important for a longitudinal intervention study and enhances transparency and credibility of the findings.

results.result: The study found that Affect training (socio-emotional/compassion-based) specifically increased CA1-3 hippocampal subfield volume compared to Perspective training, with bilateral CA1-3 showing subtle increases following Affect and subtle decreases in right CA1-3 following Perspective. No changes were observed in other subfields (SUB, CA4/DG), between Presence and control, or overall across nine months of training.
results.evaluation: Both reviewers explicitly affirm these findings. The editor states the authors 'provide convincing evidence that CA1-3 volume is sensitive to socio-emotional training,' and the anonymous reviewer confirms 'Affect training most robustly related to changes in hippocampal structure and function - specifically, CA1-3 subfields.' No concerns are raised about the structural findings.

results.result: The study identified baseline CA1-3 functional connectivity to default mode network regions (mPFC, precuneus, posterior cingulate, angular gyrus) and found differential changes following Affect versus Perspective training. Specifically, right CA1-3 showed decreased mean connectivity after Perspective, left CA1-3 showed decreased connectivity to posterior insula, and right CA1-3 showed increased connectivity to mPFC when comparing Affect to Perspective.
results.evaluation: The reviewers explicitly support these functional connectivity findings. The editor notes 'changes related to function plasticity,' and the anonymous reviewer states 'Affect training most robustly related to changes in hippocampal structure and function' and that 'change in intrinsic functional connectivity related to changes in diurnal cortisol release.' No methodological concerns are raised about the functional connectivity analyses.

results.result: Increases in bilateral CA1-3 volume following Affect training showed a negative association with changes in total diurnal cortisol output (AUCg), indicating that reductions in stress levels (measured by AUCg) were associated with increases in CA1-3 volume.
results.evaluation: Both reviewers affirm this brain-cortisol relationship. The editor states the evidence shows 'changes related to function plasticity and cortisol levels,' and the anonymous reviewer explicitly notes 'the link between CA1-3 and both short- and long-term stress changes.' The reviewers treat this as a key contribution without raising concerns.

results.result: Functional connectivity changes in CA1-3 were associated with cortisol measures: positive associations were found between left CA1-3 mean functional network and both diurnal slope and AUCg, and AUCg modulated increases in connectivity between left CA1-3 and parietal occipital area. results.result: The study's main conclusion is that only the 3-month Affect training module (cultivating compassion and care) related to increases in hippocampal CA1-3 subfield volume with corresponding alterations in functional connectivity and reductions in total diurnal cortisol output, with consistent alterations observed between cortisol change and CA1-3 volume and function across analyses.

results.result: The ReSource Project study design included 332 healthy adults randomly assigned to training cohorts (TC1, TC2) undergoing 9 months of sequential training in three modules (Presence: attention/interoceptive awareness; Affect: compassion/prosocial motivation; Perspective: metacognition/perspective-taking), an active control (TC3) with Affect only, and a retest control cohort (RCC), with assessments at baseline and after each 3-month module using MRI and physiological measures.
